ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery

Yongqiang Chen*†\dagger Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University    Chenxi Liu* Affiliation: TMLR Group, Hong Kong Baptist University    Deyu Zou* Affiliation: The Chinese University of Hong Kong    Zhenhao Chen Affiliation: MBZUAI    Tongliang Liu Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: SAIC Centre, The University of Sydney    Bo Han Affiliation: TMLR Group, Hong Kong Baptist University    Kun Zhang Affiliation: MBZUAI Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University
Abstract

Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 1111 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0×5.0\times. The improvements also transfer to 44 other LLMs and to 66 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used to build agents that operate on increasingly long-horizon tasks (Plaat et al., 2025). One of the most ambitious applications is AI scientist agents (Zheng et al., 2025a), in which LLMs automate the scientific discovery process, including literature surveys (Asai et al., 2026), hypothesis generation (Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024), data-driven analysis (Majumder et al., 2025), experiment design (Li et al., 2025a), or even the whole discovery workflow (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026; Mitchener et al., 2025). LLM-driven discovery has shown strong results in a variety of domains, such as mathematics (OpenAI, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026b), de novo protein design (Anthropic, 2026), algorithm discovery (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2026), and the research that develops LLMs themselves, an early form of recursive self-improvement (RSI) (OpenAI, 2026a; Favaro and Clark, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a; Karpathy, 2026). At the heart of the discovery loop is the iteration over scientific hypotheses, where scientific ideas compound throughout the evaluation of promising hypotheses (Wallace et al., 2026). Therefore, it is essential to reuse the discovery experience to generate high-quality hypotheses, e.g., avoiding getting stuck in repetitive mistakes or suboptimal solutions and encoding promising exploratory proposals.

In this work, we study experience reuse in open-ended discovery with evolutionary coding agents, where hypotheses are represented as solution programs to the underlying scientific problem, and experiences are accumulated as evaluated programs and their scores given by an explicit evaluator (Novikov et al., 2025). Typically, existing evolutionary coding agents such as ShinkaEvolve directly incorporate successful programs or rely on LLMs to summarize reusable insights and incorporate them as memory for future mutations with LLMs (Lange et al., 2026; Gideoni et al., 2026; Karpathy, 2026). However, program mutation contains an open-ended search space including low-level details such as hyperparameters and high-level insights such as optimization strategies. LLM-driven guidance is prone to focusing on low-level details (Karpathy, 2026; Pelleriti et al., 2026), which may not bring genuine new scientific discoveries. In contrast, human scientists tend to recognize the high-level contrasts among programs, accumulate and exploit scientific ideas from experience (Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963; Douven, 2025). The gap raises a challenging research question:

How can we reuse experience for evolutionary discovery like human scientists?

To tackle the question, we formulate evolutionary discovery as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) (Sec. 3). In each turn, the agent needs to propose meaningful solutions to uncover the underlying causal mechanism for solving the scientific problem, i.e., maximizing the evaluation score (Wallace, 1981; Glymour, ). Under the formulation, we introduce the notion of ideas as high-level mechanistic properties of the programs that determine the evaluation scores, e.g., the construction family or the optimization strategy (Def. 3.2). Without uncovering the ideas, the agent has to treat programs as unrelated and cannot tell whether a revision changes an idea or only a low-level detail, so discovery degenerates into exhaustive search (Thm. 3.1). Meanwhile, the identification of ideas also requires sufficient exploration to contrast programs with and without each idea (Thm. 3.3). Hence, an effective discovery agent needs to extract ideas from experience, and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary.

Motivated by the analysis, we propose ExpEvolve, which recognizes, structures, and leverages the high-level idea factors from discovery experience (Fig. 1). Specifically, ExpEvolve realizes the discovery of ideas via identifying high-level factors that help explain the program scoring differences. Built upon COAT (Liu et al., 2025), the discovered idea factors are expected to predict which program performs better given any pair of programs in the experience. Then, the admitted idea factors will be incorporated as an action of a multi-armed bandit that controls the exploration and exploitation of different ideas during discovery. To enable sufficient exploration, ExpEvolve also allocates slots for random exploration (Gideoni et al., 2026), and idea-guided exploration when the evolution comes to a plateau. The idea-guided exploration enforces LLMs to explore diverse ideas other than those widely used in top-scoring programs. The idea-based control in ExpEvolve allows efficient exploitation of promising ideas while continuing to explore programs with varied ideas.

We evaluate ExpEvolve on 1111 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks with a budget of 200200 evaluated programs, using SCS as the backbone and the main baseline (Sec. 5). Under two configurations that split the budget into 2020 generations of 1010 programs and 1010 generations of 2020 programs, ExpEvolve improves the final performance over SCS and ShinkaEvolve in most settings with smaller budgets up to 5.0×5.0\times. Further analyses show that the discovered idea factors order the archived programs better than their code length on all 1111 tasks. We further integrate ExpEvolve into OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) on six tasks from MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a), where it improves the mean final best-so-far score of OpenRSI on all six tasks.

2 Related Work

In this section, we discuss the closest related works and defer a more detailed one in Appendix B.

AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity and the development of agentic systems, building LLM-based AI scientists has gained increasing attention (Zhou et al., 2025). One research line automates part or the whole of the pipelines in scientific activities through agentic workflows (Lu et al., 2026; Yamada et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026b; Lyu et al., 2026b). Evolutionary coding agents are one of the most representative AI scientist agents that integrate LLMs into evolutionary search over programs scored by an explicit evaluator (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). AI scientist agents, including evolutionary coding agents, have made impact in a variety of domains, such as mathematics (OpenAI, 2026b), materials science (Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2025), biology (Anthropic, 2026), and the development of LLMs themselves, e.g., accelerating LLM training and research toward recursive self-improvement (Karpathy, 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a; OpenAI, 2026a; Favaro and Clark, 2026; Zhang et al., 2026). As generation scales up, validating the generated hypotheses becomes the main cost (Wallace et al., 2026), and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed (Si et al., 2026). The expanding paradigm of LLM-driven scientific discovery makes the reuse of experience increasingly more essential, which is central to our work.

Experience reuse in evolutionary coding agents. Existing evolutionary coding agents typically reuse experience via conditioning on evaluated programs (Novikov et al., 2025; Gideoni et al., 2026) or summarizing textual insights from programs into memory for future mutations (Lange et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2024; Volkov et al., 2026). The useful experience can also be exploited for future search control, e.g., selection inspirations across diverse strategy clusters (Lange et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026). Different from existing works that concentrate on the unit of experience as texts or programs, ExpEvolve discovers and exploits high-level idea factors to guide program mutations.

3 Theoretical Formulation of Evolutionary Discovery

In this section, we formalize evolutionary discovery and introduce the notion of ideas.

3.1 Evolutionary Discovery as a POMDP

Scientific discovery aims to uncover the causal mechanisms underlying a problem through interactions with the world (Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963). In evolutionary discovery, the agent interacts with the problem through an evaluator. We denote by θsci∈Θ\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in\Theta the hidden mechanism of the problem, which is fixed during the search and unknown to the agent. At turn tt, the agent proposes a program pt∈𝒫p_{t}\in\mathcal{P} and observes a score yty_{t} with 𝔼⁡[yt∣pt]=F⁡(pt,θsci)\mathbb{E}[y_{t}\mid p_{t}]=F(p_{t};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}), where F:𝒫×Θ→ℝF:\mathcal{P}\times\Theta\to\mathbb{R} is the objective, e.g., the value of a mathematical construction, the efficiency of a kernel, or the performance of a trained model (Novikov et al., 2025). The goal is to uncover θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} by optimizing for the evaluation score.

POMDP. As shown in Fig. 2B, the interaction forms a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) with a static hidden state st=θscis_{t}=\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}, actions at=pta_{t}=p_{t}, observations ot=yto_{t}=y_{t}, an identity transition kernel, and the observation kernel O⁡(yt∣θsci,pt)O(y_{t}\mid\theta_{\mathrm{sci}},p_{t}). Given a budget of TT evaluations, the agent chooses p0,…,pT−1p_{0},\dots,p_{T-1} to find a program p^\hat{p} with high F⁡(p^,θsci)F(\hat{p};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}).

Evaluation as intervention. θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} can be parameterized as a structural causal model over variables of interest (Spirtes et al., 2000), in which a program specifies a configuration xpx_{p} of design variables XX. Each evaluation can be considered as the expected outcome of the intervention:

F(p;θsci)=𝔼[Y|do(X=xp),θsci].F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\mathbb{E}\big[\,Y\,\big|\,\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\ \theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\big]. (1)

In this work, we leverage the causal view to provide a more in-depth understanding, while neither the analysis nor the method requires recovering the causal graph. A full discussion on the relations with causality can be found in Appendix C.

Experience-driven discovery. We define btb_{t} as the agent’s Bayesian belief after accumulating experience ht={(p0,y0),…,(pt−1,yt−1)}h_{t}=\{(p_{0},y_{0}),\dots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\}, which is essentially a probability distribution on Θ\Theta, bt​(B)=Pr⁡(Θsci∈B∣ht)b_{t}(B)=\Pr(\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in B\mid h_{t}) for B⊆ΘB\subseteq\Theta. In the ideal Bayesian formalism, the belief btb_{t} is a sufficient statistic for decision-making (Kaelbling et al., 1998). In practice, the AI Scientist maintains an internal belief within LLMs, or an external one realized as memory mt=Φ⁡(ht)m_{t}=\Phi(h_{t}) for some (possibly learnable) summarization function Φ\Phi (Lange et al., 2026), to represent the approximate representation of its knowledge about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} and the landscape of F⁡(⋅,θsci)F(\cdot;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}). Each evaluation step (pt,yt)(p_{t},y_{t}) thus updates mtm_{t}, which in turn updates the agent’s belief about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} and determines the next action pt+1p_{t+1}.

3.2 Reusing Experience with Ideas

If the evaluator fully reveals θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} and the evaluation budget is unlimited, then enumerating every possible program can directly lead to discovery. However, in reality, the evaluation score only reveals partial information about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} and evaluations can be expensive, e.g., training a model or running a physical experiment, so the agent can afford only a limited number of them (Wallace et al., 2026). Therefore, it is essential to reuse experience from past evaluations.

Without properly reusing experience, a single evaluation cannot reveal further insights about other unseen programs, and the agent then has to evaluate every candidate program to find the best one. Reusing experience requires some structure shared across programs, so that the evaluation of one program also informs the others. We formalize the contrast as follows.

Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse, informal).

Let 𝒫={p1,…,pK}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{K}\}, and let each evaluation return yt=F⁡(pt,θsci)+εty_{t}=F(p_{t};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})+\varepsilon_{t} with εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) i.i.d.

  1. (a)

    With reuse. If each program has a known representation ϕ⁡(p)∈ℝd\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖ϕ⁡(p)‖2≤1\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1 and F⁡(p,θsci)=⟨ϕ⁡(p),w⋆⟩F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\langle\phi(p),w^{\star}\rangle for an unknown w⋆∈ℝdw^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, then under a coverage condition on the representation, there exists a policy that, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, outputs a program within ϵ\epsilon of the optimal value after O⁡(d​σ2ϵ2​log⁡Kδ)O\big(d\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{K}{\delta}\big) evaluations.

  2. (b)

    Without reuse. If programs are unrelated, i.e., F⁡(pi,θsci)=μiF(p_{i};\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=\mu_{i} for an arbitrary μ∈ℝK\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, then any policy with the same guarantee for every μ\mu needs Ω⁡(K​σ2ϵ2​log⁡1δ)\Omega\big(K\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\big) evaluations.

The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix E. Theorem 3.1 implies that reusing experience at the high-level design choices can significantly improve sample efficiency from Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) to O⁡(d​log⁡K)O(d\log K), where K≫dK\gg d. In evolutionary discovery, KK counts the candidate program space, which grow combinatorially with the high-level design choices and further with the ways of implementing each choice, while dd is determined by the design choices that affect the score. Most existing agents retain experience at the level of programs (Novikov et al., 2025; Lange et al., 2026), which ignores the high-level design choices. In contrast, human scientists recognize and record what they learn from experiments in terms of reusable concepts, e.g., a construction or an optimization technique, which carry over to later experiments. We are hence inspired to introduce the notion of ideas.

Definition 3.2 (Idea).

An idea is an interpretable mapping z:𝒫→𝒱z:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{V} from programs to a binary or categorical value. It describes a high-level mechanistic property that can be shared by syntactically different programs, such as the construction family, initialization, or optimization procedure. A set of ideas {z1,…,zr}\{z_{1},\dots,z_{r}\} defines the idea representation Z⁡(p)=(z1​(p),…,zr​(p))Z(p)=(z_{1}(p),\dots,z_{r}(p)).

A program realizes a set of ideas together with low-level details. We call an idea representation ZZ faithful if the score depends on a program only through its ideas, i.e., F⁡(p,θsci)=g⁡(Z⁡(p))F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=g(Z(p)) for some function gg determined by θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}. Under a faithful idea representation, the hidden mechanism acts on a program only through its ideas, and Theorem 3.1 applies with ϕ⁡(p)\phi(p) being the one-hot encoding of Z⁡(p)Z(p), whose dimension is determined by the number of ideas.

Identifiability of ideas. However, the agent does not know in advance which representation is faithful, and the ideas have to be identified from the evaluated programs, while which programs are evaluated is decided by the search itself. When the search stops varying the candidate ideas, the exploration of ideas degenerates, as formalized below.

Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas).

Consider two candidate ideas z0z_{0} and z1z_{1}, and two mechanisms θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1} under which the score depends on z0z_{0} and z1z_{1}, respectively, i.e., F⁡(p,θi)=g⁡(Z⁡(p),zi​(p))F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p)) for a common representation ZZ and function gg, with the same observation noise. Suppose the optimal programs under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1} are different and unique with a margin Δ>0\Delta>0. Then for any policy that only evaluates programs on which z0z_{0} and z1z_{1} agree, there exists i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} such that for every budget TT, the output p^\hat{p} satisfies 𝔼⁡[maxp∈𝒫⁡F⁡(p,θi)−F⁡(p^,θi)]≥Δ/2\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F(p;\theta_{i})-F(\hat{p};\theta_{i})\big]\geq\Delta/2.

The formal statement and proof are given in Appendix F. Theorem 3.3 can be considered as a consequence of the partial observability of θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}, since the scores reveal θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} only through the evaluated programs. If two candidate ideas agree on all explored programs, the two mechanisms produce the same observations, and one cannot distinguish which idea determines the score. This situation is common in evolutionary search: as the search concentrates around its current best programs, the ideas shared by these programs stop varying. Identifying ideas thus requires sufficient exploration to contrast programs with and without each idea, to isolate contributions of ideas in the program space.

4 ExpEvolve: Discovering and Exploiting Ideas from Experience

Theoretical analysis in Sec. 3 suggests that a discovery agent should extract ideas from its experience, and keep exploring programs where the ideas vary. We realize the theoretical principles in ExpEvolve. The full procedure and implementation details are given in Alg. 1 and Appendix H.

4.1 Discovering Ideas from Experience

We leverage the discovery loop of the COAT framework (Liu et al., 2025) to find idea factors according to their theoretical properties.

Idea memory. During the discovery, ExpEvolve maintains an idea memory ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} which is a set of idea factors. Each idea factor is stored with a name, a description of its code pattern, a type, i.e., binary or categorical, and a value set 𝒱\mathcal{V}. For each program in the experience archive, the values of idea factors are annotated by an annotator LLM, which instantiates the idea representation Z⁡(p)Z(p).

Explainability of idea factors. A faithful idea representation is expected to be able to predict the score of a program, i.e., F⁡(p,θsci)=g⁡(Z⁡(p))F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}})=g(Z(p)) (Sec. 3.2). However, predicting the exact scores from ideas is difficult, since the scores of different tasks lie on different scales, the unknown function gg can be highly nonlinear, and the archive only contains a limited number of noisy evaluations. Therefore, we define the explainability of an idea representation by its pairwise predictability, i.e., whether Z⁡(p)Z(p) and Z⁡(p′)Z(p^{\prime}) predict which of two programs pp and p′p^{\prime} is better. The ranking is already informative for optimizing the objective, invariant to the scale of the scores, and more robust to noise than the scores.

Discovering idea factors from unexplained pairs. The idea discovery process in ExpEvolve is an iterative loop: each time the discovery is triggered, ExpEvolve fits a pairwise ranker on the annotated idea factors, and selects the pairs of archived programs with a large score gap that the current idea factors fail to explain. The unexplained pairs suggest the existence of missing idea factors that separate the programs in each pair. For the selected pairs, a separate proposer LLM reads the programs to propose candidate idea factors that distinguish them. Each candidate is then annotated on the whole archive, and is admitted into the idea memory if each of its values is supported by enough programs and its values separate the scores.

4.2 Exploiting Idea Factors for Discovery

We build a two-level exploration and exploitation framework with a multi-armed bandit (MAB) to fully exploit discovered idea factors while exploring varying design spaces.

Exploration and MAB exploitation. In each generation, ExpEvolve keeps at least a fraction ρ\rho of the slots for random exploration that follows SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026) with randomly sampled example programs, which explores programs beyond the current ideas and provides new material for discovery. The remaining slots are allocated to idea-guided actions by MAB.

Idea factors as MAB actions. To exploit an idea factor zz, ExpEvolve compiles it into edit actions, e.g., 𝖠𝖣𝖣⁡(z)\mathsf{ADD}(z) and 𝖱𝖤𝖬𝖮𝖵𝖤⁡(z)\mathsf{REMOVE}(z) for a binary idea factor. An action adds to the context an instruction that describes zz, together with demonstration programs in the target state, to ask the mutator LLM to realize the action in the new program. The MAB selects the action for each idea-guided slot. The reward of an action is the score of the program generated under the action relative to the random exploration in the same generation, i.e.,r=y−y¯randσrand,r=\frac{y-\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}}, where yy is the score of the generated program, and y¯rand\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}} and σrand\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}} are the mean and the standard deviation of the scores of random exploration in the same generation. The normalization removes the drift of scores across generations and the differences of score scales across tasks. The MAB selects the actions with an upper confidence bound (UCB) rule on the maximum reward of each action (Appendix H.3).

Exploration at plateaus. Oftentimes, evolutionary discovery can concentrate around its best programs and a single strategy. Consequently, the ideas widely used in top-scoring programs stop varying, and their roles cannot be identified from the archive (Thm. 3.3). When the best score does not improve for κ\kappa generations, ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration, which enforces the mutator LLM to explore diverse ideas other than those widely used in top-scoring programs. Specifically, a separate LLM probes the properties shared by the top-scoring programs as background idea factors, and an LLM judge determines which idea factors in the memory depend on the background. ExpEvolve then masks the actions of the dependent idea factors, instructs the mutator LLM to avoid them, and assigns more slots to random exploration with diversified demonstrations.

5 Experiments

We evaluate ExpEvolve on 1111 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks and further integrate it into an evolutionary agent for Machine Learning Engineering (MLE) tasks.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks. We evaluate on 1111 open-ended mathematical discovery tasks. Nine tasks are the problems studied by SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which are taken from AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), including the first and second autocorrelation inequalities, the uncertainty inequality, the Erdős minimum overlap problem, sums and differences of sets, the max–min distance ratio, the Heilbronn problem for triangles, the kissing number in 1111 dimensions, and circle packing. The other two tasks are the Hadamard matrix problem (Wang et al., 2026) and a variant of circle packing that recovers the radii by linear programming. We report the best score at the end of the budget, as the mean and standard deviation over seeds, and the best seed. Full details of the tasks are given in Appendix I.1.

Budget. Each run evaluates 200200 programs. We consider two configurations with the same budget, i.e., 1010 generations of 2020 programs as in SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026) and 2020 generations of 1010 programs, which presents more challenges to accumulating reusable knowledge from experience.

Implementation. We compare ExpEvolve with SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which is the backbone of ExpEvolve and shows competitive results against more elaborate evolutionary coding agents. We further compare with ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026), which maintains an island-based archive and summarizes the insights of recent programs with a meta-summary. Details are given in Appendix I.2. We use DeepSeek-V4-Flash by default, and each setting is run with 33 seeds. ExpEvolve uses a random-exploration fraction ρ=0.60\rho=0.60 for 2020-gen. and ρ=0.40\rho=0.40 for 1010-gen. to keep a similar number of random-exploration slots, i.e., 66 and 88. We donot tune other hyperparameters.

5.2 Main Results

ExpEvolve consistently improves the final performance. Table 1 shows the final performance at the budget of 200200 programs. ExpEvolve improves the mean and best final performances across most settings over SCS and ShinkaEvolve. Moreover, the improvements are robust to how the budget is parallelized. From 1010 generations of 2020 programs to 2020 generations of 1010 programs, the mean final score of SCS can drop dramatically because of limited capability in experience reuse, while ExpEvolve still maintains competitive performance. More details are given in Appendix J.

ExpEvolve improves sample efficiency. Fig. 6 shows the best-so-far scores along the budget on Hadamard, Sums and differences, Heilbronn, and Minimum overlap. On these four tasks, ExpEvolve needs 1.7×1.7\times to 26.2×26.2\times fewer evaluations than SCS under both configurations.

The improvements transfer to other LLMs. Fig. 7 (a) shows that the advantages of ExpEvolve over SCS transfers to other LLMs such as DeepSeek-v4-pro, GLM-5.2 and Gemini-3.7-Flash.

Summarizing experience as memory helps the early search but saturates. ShinkaEvolve and SCS+meta retain the experience as a textual summary of recent programs, which provides additional context to the mutator LLM without controlling which ideas are evaluated. Fig. 7 (b) shows that SCS+meta improves over SCS in the early stage. However, its improvement slows down afterwards while ExpEvolve keep improving. It again verifies the advantages of idea-guided evolution.

The discovered idea factors explain the order of archived programs. Following the definition of explainability in Sec. 4.1, we measure the fraction of archived program pairs that discovered factors can order correctly. As shown in Fig. 8(a), the discovered idea factors reach an accuracy of 0.790.79 to 0.990.99. Fig. 8(b) shows the idea factor with the largest weight on each task.

In an example run, idea-guided actions produce about half of the new best programs. Fig. 8(c) shows a run on Sums and differences with 1010 generations of 2020 programs. 66 of the 1111 new best programs come from idea-guided slots. The 9292 idea-guided slots of the run select 77 distinct actions, and all the new best programs from idea-guided slots come from 22 of them.

5.3 Additional Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering Tasks

We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to MLE by integrating it into OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) and evaluating it on 66 tasks from MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a): Online bandit, Anomaly detection, Clustering, Multi-objective optimization, Subgroup calibration shift, and Evolution strategy. Search leverages the scores and execution feedback from each task.

Experimental setup. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which organizes search through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators. For each task, we retain a fixed history containing 20 completed search slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline and OpenRSI equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50 additional evaluator calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search slots per generation. All program generation uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve. For each task and method, we average the final best-so-far (BSF) scores over three seeds.

Idea-guided evolution transfers to MLE tasks. Fig. 9(a) compares OpenRSI with OpenRSI+ExpEvolve across the six tasks, where ExpEvolve shows superior performance on all six tasks, with the largest gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.

Idea-guided actions produce better exploration and exploitation on MLE tasks. Fig. 9(b) and Fig. 9(c) show two concrete trajectories in the tasks of multi-objective optimization and evolution strategy, respectively. We can find that ExpEvolve can effectively discover useful ideas such as removing running ideal-point tracking (A1), removing reference-vector adaptation (A2), and adding hybrid differential-evolution variation (A3) to effectively boost the performance. When the evolution gets stuck at plateaus, exploiting useful strategies proposed by ExpEvolve in multi-objective optimization, or exploration guided by idea factors in ExpEvolve can effectively break the plateaus and lead to improvements. More details about the implementation can be found in Appendix K.1.

6 Conclusions

We introduced ExpEvolve, which structures the experience of evolutionary discovery into idea factors and reuses them to guide the search. ExpEvolve discovers idea factors from the pairs of programs that the current idea factors fail to explain, exploits them as the actions of a multi-armed bandit, and keeps exploring programs where the ideas vary, through random exploration and idea-guided exploration at plateaus. Our analysis shows that reusing a faithful idea representation reduces the number of evaluations from Ω⁡(K)\Omega(K) to O⁡(d​log⁡K)O(d\log K), and that identifying ideas requires exploring programs where the ideas vary. On 1111 mathematical discovery tasks and 66 tasks from MLS-Bench, ExpEvolve improves the final performance and the sample efficiency of evolutionary discovery under the same evaluation budget.
