Appendix A Limitations and Future directions

Due to the resource constraints, the tasks studied in this work remain limited to small-scale verification and are relatively simple. There remains a broader scope of scientific problems to be explored where verification signals can be expensive, such as biology, medicine, etc.. Meanwhile, the factor discovery can also be guided with additional background knowledge of the task.

Appendix B Related Work

In this section, we present more detailed discussions of related works in the literature.

AI Scientist agents. With the significant advancement in LLM capacity and the development of agentic systems, a rising number of works develop agents to help scientific discovery (Zheng et al., 2025a; Zhou et al., 2025; Tie et al., 2025). Some systems automate the whole research workflow, from idea generation to experimentation and paper writing (Lu et al., 2026; Yamada et al., 2025; Gottweis et al., 2026; Ghareeb et al., 2026; Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026b; Lyu et al., 2026b). One research line automates specific scientific activities, including literature review and deep research (Asai et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025b), hypothesis generation (Li et al., 2025c; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025), hypothesis verification (Li et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025a), and feedback on scientific papers (Liang et al., 2024). Another line targets data-driven discovery and machine learning engineering (Majumder et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c; Jing et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2025), as well as embodied agents in self-driving laboratories that conduct real-world experiments (Roch et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2022; Tom et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025; Mandal et al., 2025). A growing set of benchmarks evaluates the research abilities of these agents, e.g., replicating and conducting AI research (Starace et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026; Lyu et al., 2026a), generating hypotheses from inspirations (Liu et al., 2026), discovering scientific laws and equations (Zheng et al., 2026; Shojaee et al., 2025b), and conducting research tasks in biology (Laurent et al., 2024), together with broader evaluations of research abilities (Wan et al., 2026). These lines of work have made impact in mathematics (OpenAI, 2026c; OpenAI, 2026b; Bubeck et al., 2025; Woodruff et al., 2026), chemistry (Yang et al., 2026a; Boiko et al., 2023), materials science (Ghafarollahi and Buehler, 2025), earth science (Feng et al., 2026a), biology (Swanson et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Truhn et al., 2026; Anthropic, 2026), and the development of LLMs themselves (Karpathy, 2026; OpenAI, 2026a; Favaro and Clark, 2026). As generation scales up, validating the generated hypotheses becomes the main cost (Wallace et al., 2026), and ideas that look promising often degrade once executed (Si et al., 2026), which motivates us to study how to reuse experience to reduce the evaluations needed in evolutionary discovery.

Evolutionary coding agents. FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) pairs an LLM with an evaluator and a program database to discover new constructions in extremal combinatorics, and AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) extends the loop to full codebases with an ensemble of LLMs, with applications to a large set of mathematical problems (Georgiev et al., 2025). Follow-up frameworks improve the search process: OpenEvolve provides an open-source implementation (Sharma, 2025); ShinkaEvolve improves sample efficiency with parent sampling, novelty rejection, bandit-based LLM selection, and a meta-scratchpad that summarizes insights of recent programs (Lange et al., 2026); CodeEvolve and GigaEvo maintain diversity with island models and quality-diversity archives (Assumpção et al., 2025; Khrulkov et al., 2025); MCTS-AHD organizes heuristics in a Monte Carlo search tree (Zheng et al., 2025b); and AdaEvolve adapts search intensity and resource allocation from the history of improvements (Cemri et al., 2026). The paradigm has also been applied to equation discovery (Shojaee et al., 2025a) and systems research (Cheng et al., 2025). SCS shows that simply conditioning on previous solutions is competitive with more elaborate pipelines (Gideoni et al., 2026), which we adopt as the backbone and main baseline. Classical evolutionary computation also reuses experience through credit assignment over predefined units: adaptive operator selection allocates budget across operators with multi-armed bandits (Da Costa et al., 2008), quality-diversity methods maintain elites across behavior niches (Mouret and Clune, 2015) or search for novelty alone (Lehman and Stanley, 2011), and MuEvo revises the priorities of heuristic components with short-budget probing (Lv et al., 2026). In ExpEvolve, the units receiving credit are ideas discovered during the search, and plateau handling targets the ideas shared by top programs.

Learned mutators and self-improving agents. Another line trains the LLM mutator with reinforcement learning, either during evolution (Šurina et al., 2025) or at test time on a single problem (Wang et al., 2026; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026), where experience is stored in model weights. Self-improving agents such as the Darwin Gödel Machine and the Huxley-Gödel Machine evolve the code of the agent itself (Zhang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b), SATLUTION evolves a solver repository together with its own rulebase (Yu et al., 2025a), and AlphaResearch alternates between idea proposal and program verification (Yu et al., 2025b). These directions are orthogonal to ours, which uses a fixed LLM and a fixed harness.

Causality for scientific discovery. There is a long history of discussions on how to understand the world through observations (Greenland et al., 1999; Spirtes et al., 2000; Pearl, 2009). One research line is causal discovery, which learns the causal structure among variables from observational data under assumptions such as conditional independence or constrained functional forms (Spirtes et al., 1995; Shimizu et al., 2006; Hoyer et al., 2008), from interventional data and data of multiple domains (Yang et al., 2018; Brouillard et al., 2020; Mooij et al., 2020; Huang et al., 2020; Perry et al., 2022), and in the presence of latent variables (Li et al., 2025d; Li and Liu, 2025), while experiment design selects the interventions that make the causal structure identifiable (Hyttinen et al., 2013; Li et al., 2025a). Recently, LLMs have been used to construct structured variables out of unstructured data (Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b), to estimate treatment effects from unstructured data (Dhawan et al., 2024), and to propose instrumental variables (Sheth et al., 2025). Compared with these works, the variables in ExpEvolve, i.e., ideas, are constructed from unstructured programs, and are evaluated through interventions that the search itself chooses adaptively; Sec. 3.2 characterizes what such an archive can identify.

Appendix C A Causal View of the Formulation

In this section, we present a more detailed discussion of the causal view of evolutionary discovery in Sec. 3.1.

C.1 Formulation of Scientific Discovery

Scientific discovery aims to uncover the underlying scientific knowledge or the causal mechanisms from interactions with the world (Kuhn and Hawkins, 1963), which can be formulated as a Partially Observed Markov Decision Process (POMDP) (Kaelbling et al., 1998) (Fig. 10).

Scientific knowledge.

The primary objective of an AI Scientist is to uncover the underlying scientific knowledge about the task-world, represented by a latent variable Θsci∈Θ\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in\Theta, where Θ\Theta may encode causal structure, mechanisms, inductive biases, constraints, etc. Specifically, Θsci=θsci\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}=\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} can be parameterized as a Structural Causal Model (SCM) θsci=(𝒢,ℱ,PU)\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}=(\mathcal{G},\mathcal{F},P_{U}) (Spirtes et al., 2000), where 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) is a directed graph whose nodes VV represent variables of interest and whose edges EE encode direct causal dependencies; ℱ={fv}v∈V\mathcal{F}=\{f_{v}\}_{v\in V} is a collection of structural equations v=fv​(Pa⁡(v),uv)v=f_{v}(\mathrm{Pa}(v),u_{v}), where Pa⁡(v)\mathrm{Pa}(v) denotes the parents of vv in 𝒢\mathcal{G} and uvu_{v} is an exogenous noise variable; PUP_{U} is a distribution over the exogenous variables U={uv}v∈VU=\{u_{v}\}_{v\in V}.

Evaluation as intervention on SCM.

Given the SCM parametrization of θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}, we can consider that a program p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} is encoded as a particular configuration of design variables X=xpX=x_{p}. Then, FF can be implemented as

F(p;θsci):=𝔼[Y|do(X=xp),θsci],F(p;\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}):=\mathbb{E}\big[\,Y\,\big|\,\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\,\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\big],

i.e., the expected outcome under the intervention do⁡(X=xp)\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}) in the true causal model θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}. Typical implementations of FF can be the objective value of a combinatorial optimization problem, the efficiency of a kernel program, or the performance of a machine learning model (Novikov et al., 2025).

Belief as revealed knowledge.

As in Sec. 3.1, the AI Scientist maintains a memory mt=Φ⁡(ht)m_{t}=\Phi(h_{t}) as an approximate belief about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}. Each evaluation step (pt,yt)(p_{t},y_{t}) thus updates mtm_{t}, which in turn updates the agent’s effective belief about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}. In this sense, each step reveals part of the underlying scientific knowledge, which in turn determines the next action pt+1p_{t+1}.

C.2 Ideas and Causal Representation Learning

Ideas as high-level causal variables.

In the SCM view above, a program specifies a configuration xpx_{p} of design variables XX, which are low-level and high-dimensional, e.g., every line of the code. An idea zz (Definition 3.2) is a function of the program, and hence of xpx_{p}, that summarizes the design variables at a higher level. A faithful idea representation (Sec. 3.2) requires that 𝔼[Y∣do(X=xp),θsci]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathrm{do}(X=x_{p}),\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}] depends on xpx_{p} only through Z⁡(p)Z(p), i.e., interventions on the design variables that keep all ideas fixed leave the expected outcome unchanged. Hence, an intervention on the ideas is well defined at the level of expected outcomes. This condition is related to causal feature learning (Chalupka et al., 2015), which constructs macro-level causal variables by grouping the micro-level states that induce the same outcome distribution under intervention, and to causal abstraction (Rubenstein et al., 2017), which studies when a high-level causal model is consistent with a low-level one. Faithfulness is a mean-level version of these conditions, restricted to the score of interest.

Relation to causal representation learning.

Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to recover high-level causal variables from low-level observations (Schölkopf et al., 2021), where identifiability usually relies on additional information such as interventions on the latent variables (Ahuja et al., 2023). Ideas can be viewed as the high-level causal variables of programs, and the two settings differ in three aspects. (i) In CRL, the representation is usually an encoder learned from the observations, while an idea is an interpretable function of the program that an LLM can annotate, similar to how LLMs construct high-level variables from unstructured data (Liu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025b). (ii) CRL usually aims to recover all latent variables, while ideas only need to be faithful to the score. (iii) The agent decides which programs to evaluate, and an edit that changes one idea and keeps the others fixed acts as an intervention on that idea, although an LLM edit may also change other ideas. Theorem 3.3 shows that when the evaluated programs do not vary the candidate ideas, the ideas that matter cannot be identified from the scores.

C.3 Essentiality of Causal Knowledge for AI Scientists

If the evaluation revealed the scientific knowledge completely, then with more experiment turns, the agent’s revealed scientific knowledge would converge to θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}. However, the observation from the evaluation is usually only a proxy of the scientific knowledge Θsci\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}: each evaluation returns a scalar score of the program that the agent chooses to evaluate. Different hypotheses about θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}}, e.g., ones under which different ideas determine the score, can produce the same scores on all evaluated programs. For example, if all evaluated programs in circle packing share the same initialization and the same refinement, the scores cannot tell which of the two accounts for the performance. Therefore, the causal knowledge often cannot be identified from the scores of the programs explored so far, and it is essential for an AI Scientist to explore sufficiently, i.e., to evaluate programs that distinguish the competing hypotheses. We denote by esrce_{\mathrm{src}} the environment in which the evaluation is conducted.

Definition C.1 (Causal AI Scientist).

A Causal AI Scientist is an agent specified by: (i) a policy πt(⋅∣θt,esrc)\pi_{t}(\cdot\mid\theta_{t},e_{\mathrm{src}}) selecting ptp_{t}, (ii) a counterfactual / explanatory operator CF\mathrm{CF}, that answer interventional queries (e,p)(e,p) via CF⁡(θt,e,p)\mathrm{CF}(\theta_{t};e,p) as an “explanation” of predicted performance, where θt\theta_{t} is the knowledge revealed at turn tt.

Without the revealing of the causal knowledge, the discovery process suffers from significant inefficiency and suboptimality issues. We discuss the two issues more concretely below.

Evolutionary efficiency of Causal AI Scientist. The efficiency issue is characterized by Theorem 3.1. In the linear setting of Theorem 3.1, a Causal AI Scientist can be implemented via estimating the w⋆w^{\star} and optimizing for p^\hat{p} from the history, while the black-box baseline does not consider the interactions between the historical observations. Theorem 3.1 shows that, when K≫dK\gg d, which is usually the case as the space for all programs is significantly larger than the underlying SCM, encoding (correct) causal structure, e.g., a faithful idea representation, yields an exponential (or at least multiplicative) gain in sample efficiency under finite budgets. For example, if KK grows exponentially with dd, e.g., K=2dK=2^{d}, the upper bound in Theorem 3.1 grows polynomially in dd, as O⁡(d⁡(d+log⁡1δ)​σ2ϵ2)O\big(d\,(d+\log\frac{1}{\delta})\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big), while the lower bound for the black-box baseline grows exponentially in dd, as Ω⁡(2d​log⁡1δ​σ2ϵ2)\Omega\big(2^{d}\log\frac{1}{\delta}\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\big).

Sufficient exploration of Causal AI Scientist. The suboptimality issue is characterized by Theorem 3.3. Let S⊆𝒫S\subseteq\mathcal{P} be the set of programs evaluated by the agent. Two hypotheses θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1} can be distinguished from the history only if their observation models differ on some program in SS; otherwise, the history has the same distribution under both hypotheses. Under the idea-level mechanisms in Theorem 3.3, i.e., F⁡(p,θi)=g⁡(Z⁡(p),zi​(p))F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p)) for i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, the two hypotheses agree on every program where z0z_{0} and z1z_{1} agree, so only the programs where the two ideas differ can distinguish them. Intuitively, Theorem 3.3 implies that if the evaluated programs do not distinguish the corresponding θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} among {θ0,θ1}\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\}, then the solution p^\hat{p} incurs an expected regret of at least Δ/2\Delta/2 under one of them, regardless of the budget. This situation is common in evolutionary search: as the search concentrates around its current best programs, the ideas shared by these programs stop varying among the evaluated programs, and the scores cannot tell whether these ideas are the ones that matter. Hence, a Causal AI Scientist needs to explore the programs in which the competing ideas differ, so that the scores can distinguish the hypotheses. This barrier can be removed by exploration within the same evaluator, which differs from the transfer across environments discussed below.

C.4 Transfer of Scientific Knowledge across Environments

Beyond a single evaluator, the revealed scientific knowledge is also expected to transfer to other environments. If the objective function FF is static universally, then with more experiment turns, the optimized solution ptp_{t} and the agent’s revealed scientific knowledge can also be applied universally. However, the evaluation is usually conducted at some specific environment e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}, which only gives a proxy knowledge θe\theta_{e} about the scientific knowledge Θsci\Theta_{\text{sci}}. For example, the performance of a machine learning model is usually assessed on finite samples from the test distribution, and there also exist distribution shifts from the test distribution when deploying the model in the real world (Quinonero-Candela et al., 2008). Different from Θsci\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}} that characterizes the complete causal structure about the scientific problem, optimization under environment θe\theta_{e} may introduce some spurious correlations that maximize the objective value FeF_{e} (Chen et al., 2023). Therefore, to retain the optimality of p^\hat{p} beyond the source environment esrce_{\mathrm{src}} to some target etgte_{\mathrm{tgt}}, it is essential to reveal the causal knowledge and answer causal questions for an AI Scientist, e.g., through the operator CF\mathrm{CF} in Definition C.1. Let Pe(⋅∣p,θ)P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta) denote the observation model of the evaluator in environment ee, with mean Fe​(p,θ)F_{e}(p;\theta). We have the following:

Theorem C.2.

Consider esrc,etgt∈ℰe_{\mathrm{src}},e_{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\mathcal{E} and θ0,θ1∈Θ\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta such that Pesrc(⋅∣p,θ0)=Pesrc(⋅∣p,θ1)P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{0})=P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{1}) for all p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P}, and the optimal programs in etgte_{\mathrm{tgt}} under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1} are different and unique, each better than all other programs by at least Δ>0\Delta>0. Then for any policy π\pi that can interact only with esrce_{\mathrm{src}}, there exists i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} such that for every budget TT, 𝔼⁡[maxp∈𝒫⁡Fetgt​(p,θi)−Fetgt​(p^,θi)]≥Δ/2\mathbb{E}\big[\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{i})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta_{i})\big]\geq\Delta/2.

The formal description and the proof are given in Appendix G. Intuitively, Theorem C.2 implies that if the source environment does not distinguish the corresponding θsci\theta_{\mathrm{sci}} among {θ0,θ1}\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\}, then the solution p^\hat{p} solved given source environment is suboptimal in the target environment under one of them, no matter how many evaluations are made in the source environment. In the real world, it is usually the case that two machine learning models will have similar performances under the public test benchmarks, but exhibit significantly different behaviors when generalizing to distributions from other environments. Different from Theorem 3.3, this barrier cannot be removed by more exploration in the source environment, since the two hypotheses agree on every program there. We leave a full study of the transfer of scientific knowledge across environments to future work.

Appendix D Additional Technical Details

D.1 Notation

D.2 Random variable, space, and realization (to avoid notation confusion)

We use the following (standard) convention.

(i) Hypothesis space. Θ\Theta is a set that contains all candidate scientific-knowledge hypotheses.

(ii) True but unknown instance. The real world is governed by a fixed but unknown θ⋆∈Θ\theta^{\star}\in\Theta.

(iii) Bayesian view (optional but convenient). A Bayesian agent models uncertainty by treating θ⋆\theta^{\star} as a realization of a latent random variable Θsci\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}} with prior μ0\mu_{0}, i.e. Θsci∼μ0\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\sim\mu_{0} and θ⋆\theta^{\star} is one draw from it. The belief btb_{t} is simply the posterior distribution of Θsci\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}} after seeing history hth_{t}.

(iv) Does scientific knowledge change across environments? In our formulation, the underlying scientific knowledge θ⋆\theta^{\star} is static across rounds. Different environments e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E} represent different evaluation/deployment protocols (distribution shifts, constraint changes, measurement noise, private vs public tests, etc.). Formally, environments affect either the true performance map Fe​(⋅,θ)F_{e}(\cdot;\theta) and/or the observation kernel Pe(⋅∣p,θ)P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta), while θ⋆\theta^{\star} itself remains the same hidden instance.

D.3 Evaluator as an observation model (covers deterministic and stochastic evaluators)

Fix an environment e∈ℰe\in\mathcal{E}. When the agent evaluates program pp, it receives an observation y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} drawn from

y∼Pe(⋅∣p,θ⋆),y\sim P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta^{\star}),

where Pe(⋅∣p,θ)P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta) is a conditional distribution on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}.

Deterministic evaluator.

A deterministic evaluator is the special case where there exists a function geg_{e} such that

Pe(⋅∣p,θ)=δge​(p,θ)(⋅),i.e.,y=ge(p;θ⋆)a.s.P_{e}(\cdot\mid p,\theta)=\delta_{g_{e}(p;\theta)}(\cdot),\quad\text{i.e.,}\quad y=g_{e}(p;\theta^{\star})\ \text{a.s.}

In many program-evolution settings, the evaluator is designed to deterministically check validity and compute an objective score (e.g., via a verifier and a scoring routine).

Stochastic/noisy evaluator.

A common instantiation is additive noise:

y=Fe​(p,θ⋆)+ε,ε∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2),y=F_{e}(p;\theta^{\star})+\varepsilon,\qquad\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}),

but only the proof of Theorem 3.1 relies on the Gaussian form; the other results hold for any noise distribution shared by the hypotheses.

D.4 Belief and Bayes update: kernel form and undergraduate-friendly special cases

Let ht={(p0,y0),…,(pt−1,yt−1)}h_{t}=\{(p_{0},y_{0}),\dots,(p_{t-1},y_{t-1})\} be the history. The Bayesian belief (posterior) is

bt​(B)=Pr⁡(Θsci∈B∣ht,esrc),B⊆Θ.b_{t}(B)=\Pr(\Theta_{\mathrm{sci}}\in B\mid h_{t},e_{\mathrm{src}}),\qquad B\subseteq\Theta.

General Bayes update (kernel form).

After choosing ptp_{t} and observing yty_{t} in esrce_{\mathrm{src}}, the posterior is

bt+1​(B)=∫BPesrc​(d​yt∣pt,θ)​bt​(𝑑θ)∫ΘPesrc​(d​yt∣pt,θ)​bt​(𝑑θ).b_{t+1}(B)=\frac{\int_{B}P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)\,b_{t}(d\theta)}{\int_{\Theta}P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)\,b_{t}(d\theta)}. (2)

Finite hypothesis space (sum form).

If Θ={θ1,…,θN}\Theta=\{\theta_{1},\dots,\theta_{N}\} is finite and the likelihood has a pmf Pesrc​(yt∣pt,θi)P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{i}), then

bt+1​(θi)=bt​(θi)​Pesrc​(yt∣pt,θi)∑j=1Nbt​(θj)​Pesrc​(yt∣pt,θj).b_{t+1}(\theta_{i})=\frac{b_{t}(\theta_{i})\,P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{i})}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}b_{t}(\theta_{j})\,P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta_{j})}.

Continuous hypothesis space (density form).

If Pesrc​(d​y∣p,θ)P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(dy\mid p,\theta) has a density pesrc​(y∣p,θ)p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y\mid p,\theta), then

bt+1​(θ)=bt​(θ)​pesrc​(yt∣pt,θ)∫Θbt​(θ′)​pesrc​(yt∣pt,θ′)​d​θ′.b_{t+1}(\theta)=\frac{b_{t}(\theta)\,p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta)}{\int_{\Theta}b_{t}(\theta^{\prime})\,p_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(y_{t}\mid p_{t},\theta^{\prime})\,d\theta^{\prime}}.

Deterministic evaluator (indicator/filter form).

If y=gesrc​(p,θ)y=g_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(p;\theta) deterministically, then the update becomes

bt+1(dθ)∝ 1{gesrc(pt;θ)=yt}bt(dθ),b_{t+1}(d\theta)\ \propto\ \mathbf{1}\{g_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(p_{t};\theta)=y_{t}\}\,b_{t}(d\theta),

i.e. the posterior is the prior restricted to hypotheses consistent with the observed outcome.

Appendix E Proof of Theorem 3.1 (Structured experience reuse)

Throughout this section we fix a single static environment (drop ee from notation), and assume 𝒫={p1,…,pK}\mathcal{P}=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{K}\} is finite.

E.1 Protocol and performance criterion

Experiment–then–commit protocol.

A policy π\pi interacts for TT rounds. At each round t=0,…,T−1t=0,\dots,T-1 it selects a program pt∈𝒫p_{t}\in\mathcal{P} (possibly randomized) based on the past history hth_{t}, then observes yt∈ℝy_{t}\in\mathbb{R}. After TT evaluations it outputs a final recommendation p^∈𝒫\hat{p}\in\mathcal{P}.

Simple regret.

Let f⁡(p)f(p) denote the true mean performance of program pp in this environment. Define the (random) simple regret

SRT:=maxp∈𝒫⁡f⁡(p)−f⁡(p^).\mathrm{SR}_{T}:=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}f(p)\;-\;f(\hat{p}). (3)

(ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-correctness (uniform).

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). We say a policy π\pi is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-correct uniformly on a hypothesis class ℋ\mathcal{H} if for every instance in ℋ\mathcal{H},

Pr⁡(SRT≤ϵ)≥1−δ.\Pr\big(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq\epsilon\big)\geq 1-\delta.

“Uniformly” means the guarantee must hold for all instances in the class, not only on average.

E.2 Two hypothesis classes

(1) Structured class. Each program pp has a known representation ϕ⁡(p)∈ℝd\phi(p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with ‖ϕ⁡(p)‖2≤1\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1, e.g., a faithful linear idea representation ϕ⁡(p)=Z⁡(p)\phi(p)=Z(p) (Sec. 3.2). The unknown instance is a weight vector w⋆∈ℝdw^{\star}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and

f⁡(p)=⟨ϕ⁡(p),w⋆⟩.f(p)=\langle\phi(p),w^{\star}\rangle. (4)

Observations follow a Gaussian noise model

yt=f⁡(pt)+εt,εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)​i.i.d.y_{t}=f(p_{t})+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})\ \text{i.i.d.} (5)

Coverage condition. Assume there exist dd basis programs p(1),…,p(d)p^{(1)},\dots,p^{(d)} whose representations are the standard basis:

ϕ(p(i))=ei,i=1,…,d.\phi(p^{(i)})=e_{i},\qquad i=1,\dots,d. (6)

(2) Unstructured black-box class (baseline). The unknown instance is an arbitrary vector of means

μ=(μ1,…,μK)∈ℝK,f⁡(pi)=μi,\mu=(\mu_{1},\dots,\mu_{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K},\qquad f(p_{i})=\mu_{i},

and observations are

yt=μIt+εt,εt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)​i.i.d.,y_{t}=\mu_{I_{t}}+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2})\ \text{i.i.d.}, (7)

where It∈{1,…,K}I_{t}\in\{1,\dots,K\} is the index of the chosen program pt=pItp_{t}=p_{I_{t}}. Crucially, there is no assumed relation between μi\mu_{i} and μj\mu_{j} for i≠ji\neq j.

E.3 Formal statement and proof

Theorem E.1 (Formal version of Theorem 3.1).

Fix ϵ>0\epsilon>0 and δ∈(0,1/4)\delta\in(0,1/4).

  1. 1.

    (Upper bound under the structured linear class). Under equation 4–equation 6 and equation 5, there exists a policy πlin\pi_{\mathrm{lin}} such that

    Pr⁡(SRT≤2​ϵ)≥1−δwheneverT≥ 2​d​σ2ϵ2​log⁡(2​Kδ).\Pr\big(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq 2\epsilon\big)\geq 1-\delta\quad\text{whenever}\quad T\ \geq\ 2d\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{2K}{\delta}\Big).
  2. 2.

    (Lower bound for the unstructured black-box class). For the black-box class equation 7, any policy that is (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-correct uniformly for all μ∈ℝK\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{K} must satisfy

    T≥(K−1)​σ28​ϵ2​log⁡(12​δ).T\ \geq\ (K-1)\,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\,\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big).

Replacing ϵ\epsilon with ϵ/2\epsilon/2 in part (1) gives the informal statement in Theorem 3.1.

Proof.

We prove the two parts separately.

Part (1): constructive upper bound (estimate w⋆w^{\star} then commit).

Evaluate each basis program p(i)p^{(i)} exactly nn times (total T=n​dT=nd). Let y1(i),…,yn(i)y^{(i)}_{1},\dots,y^{(i)}_{n} be the observations for basis ii, and define

w^i:=1n​∑j=1nyj(i).\hat{w}_{i}:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}y^{(i)}_{j}.

By equation 4–equation 6, f⁡(p(i))=wi⋆f(p^{(i)})=w^{\star}_{i}. By equation 5, w^i∼𝒩⁡(wi⋆,σ2/n)\hat{w}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(w^{\star}_{i},\sigma^{2}/n) and these coordinates are independent.

Define for any program pp:

f^​(p):=⟨ϕ⁡(p),w^⟩,w^=(w^1,…,w^d).\widehat{f}(p):=\langle\phi(p),\hat{w}\rangle,\qquad\hat{w}=(\hat{w}_{1},\dots,\hat{w}_{d}).

Then

f^​(p)−f⁡(p)=⟨ϕ⁡(p),w^−w⋆⟩∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2n​‖ϕ⁡(p)‖22),\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)=\langle\phi(p),\hat{w}-w^{\star}\rangle\sim\mathcal{N}\!\Big(0,\ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{n}\|\phi(p)\|_{2}^{2}\Big),

so since ‖ϕ⁡(p)‖2≤1\|\phi(p)\|_{2}\leq 1,

Pr⁡(|f^​(p)−f⁡(p)|≥ϵ)≤2​exp⁡(−n​ϵ22​σ2).\Pr\big(|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\geq\epsilon\big)\leq 2\exp\!\Big(-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big).

Union bound over KK programs gives

Pr⁡(maxp∈𝒫⁡|f^​(p)−f⁡(p)|≥ϵ)≤2​K​exp⁡(−n​ϵ22​σ2).\Pr\Big(\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\geq\epsilon\Big)\leq 2K\exp\!\Big(-\frac{n\epsilon^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Big).

Choose

n≥ 2​σ2ϵ2​log⁡(2​Kδ),n\ \geq\ 2\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{2K}{\delta}\Big),

so that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta we have maxp⁡|f^​(p)−f⁡(p)|≤ϵ\max_{p}|\widehat{f}(p)-f(p)|\leq\epsilon.

Now output p^:=arg⁡maxp∈𝒫​f^​(p)\hat{p}:=\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}\widehat{f}(p). Let p⋆:=arg⁡maxp⁡f⁡(p)p^{\star}:=\arg\max_{p}f(p). On the above high-probability event,

f⁡(p⋆)−f⁡(p^)≤(f⁡(p⋆)−f^​(p⋆))+(f^​(p^)−f⁡(p^))≤ϵ+ϵ=2​ϵ.f(p^{\star})-f(\hat{p})\leq\big(f(p^{\star})-\widehat{f}(p^{\star})\big)+\big(\widehat{f}(\hat{p})-f(\hat{p})\big)\leq\epsilon+\epsilon=2\epsilon.

Thus Pr⁡(SRT≤2​ϵ)≥1−δ\Pr(\mathrm{SR}_{T}\leq 2\epsilon)\geq 1-\delta for T=n​dT=nd as stated.

Part (2): lower bound for the black-box class.

We construct KK hard instances and lower bound any uniformly (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-correct policy.

Let the programs be p1,…,pKp_{1},\dots,p_{K}. Define a base instance μ(0)∈ℝK\mu^{(0)}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}:

μ1(0)=0,μi(0)=−2ϵ(i=2,…,K).\mu^{(0)}_{1}=0,\qquad\mu^{(0)}_{i}=-2\epsilon\ \ (i=2,\dots,K).

For each i∈{2,…,K}i\in\{2,\dots,K\}, define an alternative instance μ(i)\mu^{(i)}:

μ1(i)=0,μi(i)=+2ϵ,μj(i)=−2ϵ(j∉{1,i}).\mu^{(i)}_{1}=0,\qquad\mu^{(i)}_{i}=+2\epsilon,\qquad\mu^{(i)}_{j}=-2\epsilon\ \ (j\notin\{1,i\}).

Under μ(0)\mu^{(0)}, the unique best program is p1p_{1}, and choosing any pip_{i} with i≥2i\geq 2 incurs regret 2​ϵ>ϵ2\epsilon>\epsilon. Under μ(i)\mu^{(i)}, the unique best program is pip_{i}, and choosing p1p_{1} incurs regret 2​ϵ>ϵ2\epsilon>\epsilon.

Let P0P_{0} be the distribution of the full transcript 𝒯:=(p0:T−1,y0:T−1,p^)\mathcal{T}:=(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p}) under μ(0)\mu^{(0)}, and PiP_{i} the analogous distribution under μ(i)\mu^{(i)}. Uniform (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-correctness implies

P0(p^=p1)≥1−δ,Pi(p^=p1)≤δ(i=2,…,K).P_{0}(\hat{p}=p_{1})\geq 1-\delta,\qquad P_{i}(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq\delta\quad(i=2,\dots,K).

Step 1: a KL lower bound from an event. For any event AA and distributions P,QP,Q, one has

KL(P∥Q)≥P(A)logP⁡(A)Q⁡(A)+(1−P(A))log1−P⁡(A)1−Q⁡(A).\mathrm{KL}(P\|Q)\geq P(A)\log\frac{P(A)}{Q(A)}+(1-P(A))\log\frac{1-P(A)}{1-Q(A)}.

Apply it with A={p^=p1}A=\{\hat{p}=p_{1}\}, P=P0P=P_{0}, Q=PiQ=P_{i}. Let p:=P0​(A)≥1−δp:=P_{0}(A)\geq 1-\delta and q:=Pi​(A)≤δq:=P_{i}(A)\leq\delta. For δ∈(0,1/4)\delta\in(0,1/4) this yields

KL(P0∥Pi)≥log(12​δ).\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i})\ \geq\ \log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big). (8)

Step 2: compute KL(P0∥Pi)\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i}) via number of pulls of arm ii. Under μ(0)\mu^{(0)} and μ(i)\mu^{(i)}, the policy is identical; only observations when playing pip_{i} differ:

y∼𝒩⁡(−2​ϵ,σ2)​under ​μ(0),y∼𝒩⁡(+2​ϵ,σ2)​under ​μ(i).y\sim\mathcal{N}(-2\epsilon,\sigma^{2})\ \text{under }\mu^{(0)},\qquad y\sim\mathcal{N}(+2\epsilon,\sigma^{2})\ \text{under }\mu^{(i)}.

For Gaussians with equal variance, KL(𝒩(m0,σ2)∥𝒩(m1,σ2))=(m0−m1)22​σ2\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}(m_{0},\sigma^{2})\|\mathcal{N}(m_{1},\sigma^{2}))=\frac{(m_{0}-m_{1})^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}, so each pull of pip_{i} contributes KL (4​ϵ)22​σ2=8​ϵ2σ2\frac{(4\epsilon)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}=\frac{8\epsilon^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}.

Let NiN_{i} be the (random) number of times pip_{i} is evaluated in TT rounds. Additivity of log-likelihood ratios over independent Gaussian samples yields

KL(P0∥Pi)=8​ϵ2σ2𝔼P0[Ni].\mathrm{KL}(P_{0}\|P_{i})=\frac{8\epsilon^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\ \mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}]. (9)

Step 3: conclude the lower bound on TT. Combine equation 8 and equation 9:

𝔼P0[Ni]≥σ28​ϵ2log(12​δ),i=2,…,K.\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}]\ \geq\ \frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big),\qquad i=2,\dots,K.

Summing over i=2,…,Ki=2,\dots,K gives

T=∑i=1KNi≥∑i=2K𝔼P0​[Ni]≥(K−1)​σ28​ϵ2​log⁡(12​δ).T=\sum_{i=1}^{K}N_{i}\ \geq\ \sum_{i=2}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{P_{0}}[N_{i}]\ \geq\ (K-1)\frac{\sigma^{2}}{8\epsilon^{2}}\log\!\Big(\frac{1}{2\delta}\Big).

This completes the proof. ∎

Remark (deterministic evaluator).

If σ=0\sigma=0, the structured linear class can recover w⋆w^{\star} exactly from dd basis evaluations and achieve SRT=0\mathrm{SR}_{T}=0, while in the unstructured black-box class a uniform worst-case guarantee requires evaluating all KK programs at least once.

Relation to best-arm identification.

The lower bound follows the standard change-of-measure argument for best-arm identification in KK-armed Gaussian bandits (Kaufmann et al., 2016), and the upper bound is a simple instance of best-arm identification in linear bandits (Soare et al., 2014).

Appendix F Proof of Theorem 3.3 (Degenerated exploration of ideas)

F.1 Formal statement and proof

For a policy that interacts for TT rounds and outputs p^\hat{p}, define the simple regret under mechanism θ\theta as SRT​(θ)≔maxp∈𝒫⁡F⁡(p,θ)−F⁡(p^,θ)\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta)\coloneqq\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F(p;\theta)-F(\hat{p};\theta).

Theorem F.1 (Formal version of Theorem 3.3).

Let z0,z1:𝒫→𝒱z_{0},z_{1}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{V} be two ideas, and let A≔{p∈𝒫:z0​(p)=z1​(p)}A\coloneqq\{p\in\mathcal{P}:z_{0}(p)=z_{1}(p)\} be the set of programs on which they agree. Assume there exist θ0,θ1∈Θ\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta such that:

  1. (i)

    (Idea-level mechanisms) F⁡(p,θi)=g⁡(Z⁡(p),zi​(p))F(p;\theta_{i})=g(Z(p),z_{i}(p)) for all p∈𝒫p\in\mathcal{P} and i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, for a common representation ZZ and function gg, and each evaluation returns y=F⁡(p,θi)+εy=F(p;\theta_{i})+\varepsilon with the same noise distribution under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1};

  2. (ii)

    (Optimal program flips with margin Δ\Delta) there exist p0≠p1p_{0}\neq p_{1} and Δ>0\Delta>0 such that F⁡(pi,θi)−F⁡(p,θi)≥ΔF(p_{i};\theta_{i})-F(p;\theta_{i})\geq\Delta for all p≠pip\neq p_{i} and i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}.

Then for any policy that only evaluates programs in AA, there exists i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} such that for every budget TT,

𝔼⁡[SRT​(θi)]≥Δ/2.\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{i})\big]\ \geq\ \Delta/2.

Moreover, at least one of p0p_{0} and p1p_{1} lies outside AA.

Proof.

For every p∈Ap\in A, z0​(p)=z1​(p)z_{0}(p)=z_{1}(p) gives F⁡(p,θ0)=g⁡(Z⁡(p),z0​(p))=g⁡(Z⁡(p),z1​(p))=F⁡(p,θ1)F(p;\theta_{0})=g(Z(p),z_{0}(p))=g(Z(p),z_{1}(p))=F(p;\theta_{1}). Together with the common noise distribution in (i), the observation model O(⋅∣θi,p)O(\cdot\mid\theta_{i},p) is identical under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1} for every p∈Ap\in A.

Let ℙi\mathbb{P}_{i} be the distribution of the transcript (p0:T−1,y0:T−1,p^)(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p}) when the true mechanism is θi\theta_{i}. Since the policy only evaluates programs in AA, for any history and any chosen pt∈Ap_{t}\in A, the conditional distribution of yty_{t} is identical under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1}, and the policy chooses pt+1p_{t+1} and p^\hat{p} with the same randomization given the same history. By induction on tt, ℙ0=ℙ1\mathbb{P}_{0}=\mathbb{P}_{1}. In particular, the output p^\hat{p} has the same distribution QQ on 𝒫\mathcal{P} under both mechanisms.

By (ii), any output p^≠pi\hat{p}\neq p_{i} incurs regret at least Δ\Delta under θi\theta_{i}, so

𝔼⁡[SRT​(θ0)]≥Δ⁡(1−Q⁡(p^=p0)),𝔼⁡[SRT​(θ1)]≥Δ⁡(1−Q⁡(p^=p1)).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{0})]\ \geq\ \Delta\,\big(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})\big),\qquad\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{SR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\ \geq\ \Delta\,\big(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\big).

Since p0≠p1p_{0}\neq p_{1}, Q⁡(p^=p0)+Q⁡(p^=p1)≤1Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})+Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq 1, so at least one of the two probabilities is at most 1/21/2, and the corresponding expected regret is at least Δ/2\Delta/2.

For the last claim, suppose both p0,p1∈Ap_{0},p_{1}\in A. Then F⁡(p1,θ0)=F⁡(p1,θ1)≥F⁡(p0,θ1)+Δ=F⁡(p0,θ0)+ΔF(p_{1};\theta_{0})=F(p_{1};\theta_{1})\geq F(p_{0};\theta_{1})+\Delta=F(p_{0};\theta_{0})+\Delta, which contradicts the optimality of p0p_{0} under θ0\theta_{0}. ∎

The theorem holds for any budget, since the barrier comes from the programs that the policy evaluates. To identify which of z0z_{0} and z1z_{1} matters, the policy has to evaluate a program outside AA, i.e., a program on which the two ideas differ. In ExpEvolve, this is the role of plateau-aware revision, which changes the proposal distribution to evaluate programs where the ideas shared by the leading programs differ.

Appendix G Proof of Theorem C.2 (Non-identifiability under environment shifts)

G.1 Setup: source interaction, target evaluation, and target regret

The agent can only interact with the source environment esrce_{\mathrm{src}}:

yt∼Pesrc(⋅∣pt,θ⋆).y_{t}\sim P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p_{t},\theta^{\star}).

After TT rounds it outputs a final program p^\hat{p}. Performance is judged in a target environment etgte_{\mathrm{tgt}} via Fetgt​(p,θ⋆)F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta^{\star}). Define the target (simple) regret:

GRT​(θ⋆):=maxp∈𝒫⁡Fetgt​(p,θ⋆)−Fetgt​(p^,θ⋆).\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta^{\star}):=\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta^{\star})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta^{\star}).

G.2 Formal statement and proof

Theorem G.1 (Non-identifiability barrier under shifts).

Fix esrc,etgt∈ℰe_{\mathrm{src}},e_{\mathrm{tgt}}\in\mathcal{E}. Assume there exist two hypotheses θ0,θ1∈Θ\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\in\Theta such that:

(Source indistinguishability)Pesrc(⋅∣p,θ0)=Pesrc(⋅∣p,θ1),∀p∈𝒫.\displaystyle\textbf{(Source indistinguishability)}\quad P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{0})=P_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}(\cdot\mid p,\theta_{1}),\quad\forall p\in\mathcal{P}. (10)
(Target optimal action flips with margin Δ)∃p0,p1∈𝒫​and​Δ>0​s.t.\displaystyle\textbf{(Target optimal action flips with margin $\Delta$)}\quad\exists\,p_{0},p_{1}\in\mathcal{P}\ \text{and}\ \Delta>0\ \text{s.t.} (11)
p0∈arg⁡maxp∈𝒫​Fetgt​(p,θ0),p1∈arg⁡maxp∈𝒫​Fetgt​(p,θ1),\displaystyle\qquad p_{0}\in\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{0}),\quad p_{1}\in\arg\max_{p\in\mathcal{P}}F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{1}),
Fetgt​(p0,θ0)−Fetgt​(p,θ0)≥Δ,∀p≠p0,Fetgt​(p1,θ1)−Fetgt​(p,θ1)≥Δ,∀p≠p1.\displaystyle\qquad F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{0};\theta_{0})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{0})\geq\Delta,\ \forall p\neq p_{0},\quad F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{1};\theta_{1})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p;\theta_{1})\geq\Delta,\ \forall p\neq p_{1}. (12)

Then for any policy π\pi that can interact only with esrce_{\mathrm{src}}, there exists i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\} such that for every budget TT,

𝔼⁡[GRT​(θi)]≥Δ/2.\mathbb{E}\big[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{i})\big]\ \geq\ \Delta/2.

This impossibility holds whether the evaluator is stochastic or deterministic, since equation 10 is stated at the level of the full observation model PesrcP_{e_{\mathrm{src}}}.

Proof.

Let ℙi\mathbb{P}_{i} be the distribution over the full transcript

𝒯:=(p0:T−1,y0:T−1,p^)\mathcal{T}:=(p_{0:T-1},y_{0:T-1},\hat{p})

when the true hypothesis is θi\theta_{i} and interaction is only with esrce_{\mathrm{src}}.

By equation 10, for any history and any chosen action ptp_{t}, the conditional distribution of yty_{t} is identical under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1}. By induction on tt, the entire transcript distribution is identical:

ℙ0=ℙ1.\mathbb{P}_{0}=\mathbb{P}_{1}.

In particular, the marginal distribution of the final output p^\hat{p} is the same under θ0\theta_{0} and θ1\theta_{1}. Let this common distribution be denoted by QQ on 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Now consider the expected target regret under θ0\theta_{0}: by equation 12, any output p^≠p0\hat{p}\neq p_{0} incurs regret at least Δ\Delta under θ0\theta_{0}:

GRT(θ0)=Fetgt(p0;θ0)−Fetgt(p^;θ0)≥Δ⋅𝟏{p^≠p0}.\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})=F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(p_{0};\theta_{0})-F_{e_{\mathrm{tgt}}}(\hat{p};\theta_{0})\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot\mathbf{1}\{\hat{p}\neq p_{0}\}.

Taking expectation w.r.t. QQ yields

𝔼⁡[GRT​(θ0)]≥Δ⋅(1−Q⁡(p^=p0)).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})]\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})).

Similarly,

𝔼⁡[GRT​(θ1)]≥Δ⋅(1−Q⁡(p^=p1)).\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\ \geq\ \Delta\cdot(1-Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})).

Since Q⁡(p^=p0)+Q⁡(p^=p1)≤1Q(\hat{p}=p_{0})+Q(\hat{p}=p_{1})\leq 1, at least one of these probabilities is at most 1/21/2, so at least one of the two expected regrets is at least Δ/2\Delta/2:

max⁡{𝔼⁡[GRT​(θ0)],𝔼⁡[GRT​(θ1)]}≥Δ/2.\max\{\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{0})],\ \mathbb{E}[\mathrm{GR}_{T}(\theta_{1})]\}\ \geq\ \Delta/2.

This proves the claim. ∎

G.3 Concrete examples satisfying the conditions

We give two illustrative examples where source data cannot distinguish two hypotheses, yet the target-optimal decision differs.

Example 1: public test vs private (distribution shift / shortcut feature).

Let θ∈{θ0,θ1}\theta\in\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1}\} encode which feature is truly stable/causal. Programs correspond to two model families: p0p_{0} uses a stable causal feature; p1p_{1} uses a shortcut feature. In the source environment (public benchmark), the shortcut feature is perfectly correlated with labels, so both hypotheses yield the same evaluator distribution for every program, satisfying equation 10. In the target environment (deployment/private), the shortcut correlation breaks: under θ0\theta_{0}, p0p_{0} is uniquely optimal; under θ1\theta_{1}, p1p_{1} is uniquely optimal, with margin Δ\Delta, satisfying equation 12. No amount of interaction with esrce_{\mathrm{src}} can identify which world holds.

Example 2: relaxed verification (slack) vs exact verification (constraint shift).

In combinatorial optimization, it is common to evaluate candidate programs using a relaxed verifier (e.g., allowing numerical slack), then validate with an exact verifier. For instance, in circle packing, one may verify non-overlap with a numerical slack such as 10−610^{-6}, and later validate with an exact checker; converting a relaxed-feasible solution into an exact-feasible one may require tiny but nonzero modifications, and rankings can change when switching verifiers. This is explicitly discussed in the context of circle packing verification with slack vs exact validation. The source environment esrce_{\mathrm{src}} can correspond to the relaxed evaluator, while the target environment etgte_{\mathrm{tgt}} corresponds to the exact evaluator. Then two hypotheses θ0,θ1\theta_{0},\theta_{1} can be constructed so that they are indistinguishable under the relaxed evaluator for all queried programs, yet the exact evaluator reverses which program is truly best (with gap Δ\Delta), matching Theorem G.1.

Appendix H Implementation Details of ExpEvolve

This section describes the implementation of ExpEvolve used in our experiments. Alg. 1 summarizes the search loop, and Alg. 2 details the discovery of idea factors. We implement ExpEvolve on the backbone of SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026). In each generation, ExpEvolve generates BB programs in parallel slots. The prompt of each slot contains the task instruction, an optional strategy instruction from an idea-guided action, a summary of the idea memory, and a few example programs, and the mutator LLM GG writes a new program from the prompt. All LLM calls use DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and the hyperparameters are listed in Table 3. Each generated program is evaluated once. A program is treated as failed if the evaluation fails or returns a non-finite objective, and failed programs are neither repaired nor retried. The LLM calls for generation are not retried in our experiments either, so a failed call, e.g., due to rate limits, yields a failed program that still counts toward the evaluation budget.

H.1 Idea Memory and Annotation

Idea factors. Each idea factor zz in the idea memory ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} is stored with a name, a description of its code pattern, a type, i.e., binary or categorical, and a value set 𝒱\mathcal{V}. The description is also used by the annotator LLM to recognize the idea factor from the source code. The annotator LLM labels each program with z⁡(p)∈𝒱∪{𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇}z(p)\in\mathcal{V}\cup\{\mathsf{unknown}\}, where the label is 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown} if the idea factor cannot be recognized. The annotation of a program is a separate LLM call, independent of the proposal of idea factors, with the source code truncated to 40004000 characters.

Score contrast. For a binary idea factor, the score contrast is the difference of the mean scores between the successful programs labeled 𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾\mathsf{true} and those labeled 𝖿𝖺𝗅𝗌𝖾\mathsf{false}. For a categorical idea factor, the score contrast is the difference of the mean scores between the value with the highest mean score and the value with the lowest mean score. Programs labeled 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown} are excluded from the score contrast.

Updating the memory. After each generation, UpdateMemory labels the new programs with all existing idea factors, recomputes the score contrasts, and merges two idea factors if the Pearson correlation of their labels on the archive exceeds 0.850.85 (Alg. 1, line 8). Degenerate evaluations, whose scores collapse to extreme values, are excluded from the statistics. It also updates the statistics of the actions (Appendix H.3).

Memory summary in the prompt. Every slot, including random exploration, receives a summary of the idea memory (line 5). The summary lists the six idea factors with the largest absolute score contrasts, each with its name, description, direction of effect, numbers of programs with and without it, and score contrast, and gives the mean score of each value for categorical idea factors. It also contains the outlier programs that the current idea factors fail to explain, i.e., one program with a large positive residual and one with a large negative residual (|z|≥1.5|z|\geq 1.5), with their source code truncated to 15001500 characters.

H.2 Idea Discovery

Trigger. Discovery is triggered every ndiscn_{\mathrm{disc}} generations after the first generation, when the archive contains at least 1515 successful programs and the idea memory contains fewer than 1212 idea factors, excluding the background idea factors (Alg. 1, line 9).

Pairwise ranker. Let σY\sigma_{Y} be the standard deviation of the scores of the successful programs in the archive. ExpEvolve builds all pairs of successful programs (p,p′)(p,p^{\prime}) with |y⁡(p)−y⁡(p′)|≥0.25​σY|y(p)-y(p^{\prime})|\geq 0.25\,\sigma_{Y}, and labels each pair by sign⁡(y⁡(p)−y⁡(p′))\mathrm{sign}(y(p)-y(p^{\prime})). The feature of a pair is the difference of the binary encodings of the idea factors, where a factor is encoded as 11 if it is labeled 𝗍𝗋𝗎𝖾\mathsf{true} and 00 otherwise, together with the standardized difference of the code lengths as a covariate. The ranker is a ridge least-squares model without intercept (λ=10−3\lambda=10^{-3}), refit in each discovery round.

Selecting unexplained pairs. ExpEvolve selects the pairs that the ranker orders incorrectly (Alg. 2, line 4), and excludes the pairs on which the current idea factors take identical values. The selected pairs are ranked by acc0​(p,p′)⋅w⁡(p,p′)\mathrm{acc}_{0}(p,p^{\prime})\cdot w(p,p^{\prime}), where w⁡(p,p′)=1.5w(p,p^{\prime})=1.5 if the two programs come from the same generation and 11 otherwise. The null accuracy acc0​(p,p′)\mathrm{acc}_{0}(p,p^{\prime}) is the fraction of 500500 random permutations of the scores over programs, under which a ranker refit on the permuted labels still predicts the true order of the pair. A pair with a high null accuracy is easy to order from the idea factors, so that its misranking indicates a missing idea factor. The null accuracy uses the differences of the idea factors without the code-length covariate. Up to ℓ=6\ell=6 pairs are used, with each program appearing in at most two pairs. If fewer than 33 pairs are available, the discovery round is skipped. When the idea memory is empty, ExpEvolve selects the ℓ\ell pairs with the largest score gaps under the same constraints (lines 1–2).

Proposing candidates. For each selected pair, the prompt of the proposer LLM contains the score gap in raw units and in units of σY\sigma_{Y}, the scores, the predicted scores and the residuals of both programs, the order predicted by the ranker, the idea factors on which the two programs differ, and the source code of both programs truncated to 15001500 characters each. The proposer LLM is asked to explain the unexpected order, and proposes 88 candidates in each round, each with a name, a description, a type, a value set, and a predicted direction (line 6).

Annotation and admission. Each candidate is annotated on the whole archive (line 8). ExpEvolve admits a candidate if the two values compared by its score contrast are each taken by at least nmin=5n_{\min}=5 programs, the absolute score contrast is at least η=max⁡(0.25​σY, 10−3)\eta=\max(0.25\,\sigma_{Y},\,10^{-3}), and the candidate does not duplicate an idea factor in the memory, an idea factor removed before, or another selected candidate (line 9). Two idea factors are considered duplicates if their names are identical, the token Jaccard similarity of their names is at least 0.60.6, or the token overlap of their descriptions is at least 0.450.45. Since the archive is collected adaptively by the search, the score contrast is an association within the archive and does not identify the effect of the idea factor. Admission therefore makes an idea factor available for testing, and the search examines it through the actions (Appendix H.3).

H.3 Idea-Guided Actions

Actions. Allocate compiles the idea factors into actions, i.e., 𝖠𝖣𝖣⁡(z)\mathsf{ADD}(z) and 𝖱𝖤𝖬𝖮𝖵𝖤⁡(z)\mathsf{REMOVE}(z) for a binary idea factor, and 𝖲𝖤𝖳⁡(z=v)\mathsf{SET}(z{=}v) for each value vv of a categorical idea factor (Alg. 1, line 3). The action set is rebuilt in every generation, and keeps at most three actions of the idea factors with the largest absolute score contrasts, together with a baseline action without instruction. An action that has stayed in the action set for NrotN_{\mathrm{rot}} consecutive generations is rotated out to give way to other actions, and its records are kept for when it enters the action set again. Before an admitted idea factor is compiled into actions, its absolute score contrast must exceed the 9595th percentile of a null distribution obtained from 200200 permutations of the scores, and a threshold on the absolute score contrast is used instead when the permutation test cannot be run. Background idea factors (Appendix H.4) are not compiled into actions, until they satisfy the admission conditions of Appendix H.2 and are promoted to regular idea factors.

Prompt of an action. An idea-guided slot differs from random exploration in two parts of the prompt (line 5). First, a strategy instruction asks the mutator LLM to use or avoid the pattern of zz, or to set zz to vv, with the description of zz and its estimated effect. Second, the example programs consist of the best program in the archive as an anchor, followed by the best programs in the target state of the action, where ties between programs with similar scores are broken in favor of programs with rare combinations of idea factors, and k=3k=3 example programs are used in total. There is no explicit parent program, since SCS conditions the mutator LLM on a set of example programs.

Random exploration. A random exploration slot uses the prompt of SCS without strategy instruction, with 33 example programs sampled uniformly at random from the successful programs, and the summary of the idea memory.

Diversification in the warm-up. In the warm-up generations, the slots of the baseline action in the second half of each generation receive a diversification instruction, which asks the mutator LLM to first list three to five distinct families of well-established approaches to the task as code comments, and to note which families the example programs use.

Allocating slots. In each generation, Allocate assigns max⁡(2,round⁡(ρ​B))\max(2,\mathrm{round}(\rho B)) slots to random exploration, and the remaining slots to idea-guided actions, where ut,bu_{t,b} denotes the action of slot bb and ut,b=⊥u_{t,b}=\bot denotes random exploration (line 3). An idea-guided slot falls back to random exploration if no action is available, e.g., before any idea factor is admitted, or if the actions have reached the limit of slots per generation. The fraction of random exploration is thus at least ρ\rho.

Bandit. The bandit selects the actions of idea-guided slots with a soft UCB rule,

s⁡(a)=r~max​(a)+c​ln⁡(Ntot+1)na,Pr⁡(a)∝exp⁡(s⁡(a)),s(a)=\tilde{r}_{\max}(a)+c\sqrt{\frac{\ln(N_{\mathrm{tot}}+1)}{n_{a}}},\qquad\Pr(a)\propto\exp\big(s(a)\big),

where nan_{a} is the number of times that aa has been selected, Ntot=∑anaN_{\mathrm{tot}}=\sum_{a}n_{a}, and c=1c=1. Actions that have not been selected are tried first. The value r~max​(a)\tilde{r}_{\max}(a) is the maximum reward of aa, minus a bootstrap estimate of the expected maximum of nan_{a} rewards drawn from all actions, which corrects the growth of the maximum with the number of samples. The reward of a program generated under an action follows the normalized reward in Sec. 4.2, where the standard deviation is lower bounded as σrand=max⁡(std⁡(yrand), 0.05​|y¯rand|, 10−6)\sigma_{\mathrm{rand}}=\max\big(\mathrm{std}(y_{\mathrm{rand}}),\,0.05\,|\bar{y}_{\mathrm{rand}}|,\,10^{-6}\big) (line 8). If fewer than two random exploration programs are available in the generation, the adjacent generations are included. A failed program receives a penalty score below the worst successful program.

H.4 Idea-Guided Exploration at Plateaus

Entering and leaving a plateau. ExpEvolve records the best-so-far score at the end of each generation, and the search is in a plateau if the best-so-far scores of the last κ+1\kappa+1 generations are equal up to a relative tolerance of 10−410^{-4}, after the warm-up generations. When the search enters a plateau, ReviseAtPlateau runs the background probe and the dependency judge below (Alg. 1, lines 12–13). The plateau ends as soon as the best-so-far score improves, and all the changes during the plateau are reverted in the same generation. Each time the search enters a plateau again, the probe and the judge are run again, since the background of a new plateau can differ from the previous one.

Background probe. An LLM reads the 88 successful programs with the highest scores, with the source code truncated to 15001500 characters and the names of the current idea factors, and proposes 22 to 44 binary properties that these programs share. Each property is annotated on the archive, and is recorded as a background idea factor if at least 55 of the 88 top programs are annotated and at least 80%80\% of them realize the property. A background idea factor stays in the memory after the plateau, and is promoted to a regular idea factor once enough programs without it appear in the archive and its score contrast passes the admission threshold.

Dependency judge. The background is described by the three idea factors with the largest absolute score contrasts. For each idea factor in the memory, and for each value of a categorical idea factor, an LLM judge decides, with three calls, whether it depends on the background, i.e., loses its meaning or reverses its effect once the defining property of the background no longer holds.

Changes during a plateau. While the search is in a plateau, ExpEvolve applies the following changes.

  • •

    Reversing and masking actions. For a binary idea factor judged dependent, 𝖠𝖣𝖣⁡(z)\mathsf{ADD}(z) is replaced by 𝖱𝖤𝖬𝖮𝖵𝖤⁡(z)\mathsf{REMOVE}(z) in the action set, with the same description and score contrast, so that the bandit can only move away from zz. For a categorical idea factor, the actions of the values judged dependent are masked, while the other values are kept as escape actions. The dependent idea factors are also removed from the summary of the idea memory. After the plateau, the original actions are restored, and the records of the reversed and masked actions are kept.

  • •

    Stall note. A note on the current state is prepended to the prompt of every slot. The note reports the best score and the number of generations without improvement, lists the dependent idea factors with their names and shortened descriptions, states that the search has stalled on this combination, and asks whether other constructions or combinations can reach a higher score.

  • •

    More random exploration. Each idea-guided slot is reassigned to random exploration with probability 0.90.9. Since the judge runs at the end of the first plateau generation, the probability is lowered to 0.30.3 from the next generation.

  • •

    Diversified demonstrations. Random exploration uses the best program of the background as the first example, and fills the other examples with programs outside the background, which are selected greedily to diversify their idea factors. A program is considered in the background if it realizes any dependent idea factor.

  • •

    Exploration of the bandit. In the first 22 generations of a plateau, the bandit selects the actions by the exploration bonus only.

Appendix I Experimental Details

I.1 Tasks

Table 4 summarizes the 1111 tasks. Nine tasks are the mathematical problems studied by SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which are taken from AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025), and we report their reference values as collected by Gideoni et al. (2026). All methods use the same evaluator for each task, and each evaluation is limited to 6060 seconds, except the uncertainty inequality with 300300 seconds.

First autocorrelation inequality. Let C1C_{1} be the largest constant such that maxt⁡(f∗f)​(t)≥C1​(∫f)2\max_{t}(f*f)(t)\geq C_{1}\big(\int f\big)^{2} for all non-negative functions ff supported on [−1/4,1/4][-1/4,1/4], where f∗ff*f is the autoconvolution. A non-negative step function ff gives an upper bound C1≤maxt⁡(f∗f)​(t)/(∫f)2C_{1}\leq\max_{t}(f*f)(t)/(\int f)^{2}, which the task minimizes. The number of steps is chosen by the program, and for a step function with nn steps and values hh, the score is computed as 2​n​max⁡(h∗h)/(∑h)22n\max(h*h)/(\sum h)^{2}, which is invariant to the scale of hh.

Second autocorrelation inequality. Let C2C_{2} be the smallest constant such that ‖f∗f‖22≤C2​‖f∗f‖1​‖f∗f‖∞\|f*f\|_{2}^{2}\leq C_{2}\,\|f*f\|_{1}\,\|f*f\|_{\infty} for all non-negative functions ff. A non-negative step function ff gives a lower bound C2≥‖f∗f‖22/(‖f∗f‖1​‖f∗f‖∞)C_{2}\geq\|f*f\|_{2}^{2}/(\|f*f\|_{1}\|f*f\|_{\infty}), which the task maximizes. The evaluator rejects step functions with more than 10410^{4} steps.

Uncertainty inequality. For a function gg, let A⁡(g)=inf{r>0:g⁡(x)≥0​ for all ​|x|≥r}A(g)=\inf\{r>0:g(x)\geq 0\text{ for all }|x|\geq r\}. For even functions ff with f⁡(0)≤0f(0)\leq 0 and f^​(0)≤0\hat{f}(0)\leq 0, the task minimizes A⁡(f)​A​(f^)A(f)A(\hat{f}), which upper bounds the largest constant CC such that A⁡(f)​A​(f^)≥CA(f)A(\hat{f})\geq C. Following the reformulation of Gideoni et al. (2026), ff is a Hermite–Gaussian expansion over the monic (probabilist’s) Hermite polynomials H0,H4,…,H28H_{0},H_{4},\dots,H_{28} with 77 free coefficients, which represents a larger class of functions than the original formulation over H0,H4,H8,H12H_{0},H_{4},H_{8},H_{12} with 33 free coefficients. The sign conditions are checked on a grid of 2×1052\times 10^{5} points in [10−6,30][10^{-6},30], which is refined to 2×1062\times 10^{6} points with extended precision when the score is below 0.60.6, and each evaluation is limited to 300300 seconds. Since the reformulation enlarges the search space, the resulting values are not comparable with the values of the original formulation in Table 4. In the implementation, the score is r2/(2​π)r^{2}/(2\pi), where rr is the largest root at which ff changes sign.

Erdős minimum overlap problem. For a partition of {1,…,2​n}\{1,\dots,2n\} into two sets AA and BB of equal size, let M⁡(n)=minA,B⁡maxk​|{(a,b)∈A×B:a−b=k}|M(n)=\min_{A,B}\max_{k}|\{(a,b)\in A\times B:a-b=k\}|. The task constructs a step function hh with values in [0,1][0,1], whose number of steps is chosen by the program, and minimizes the upper bound on limn→∞M⁡(n)/n\lim_{n\to\infty}M(n)/n given by twice the maximum correlation between hh and 1−h1-h divided by the number of steps.

Sums and differences of sets. Following the framework of Gyarmati, Hennecart, and Ruzsa, the task constructs a set U⊂ℕ≥0U\subset\mathbb{N}_{\geq 0} with 0∈U0\in U that maximizes θ⁡(U)=1+log⁡(|U−U|/|U+U|)/log⁡(2​max⁡(U)+1)\theta(U)=1+\log(|U-U|/|U+U|)/\log(2\max(U)+1), which lower bounds the largest exponent θ\theta such that |A−B|≥c⁡(K)​|A+B|θ|A-B|\geq c(K)|A+B|^{\theta} for arbitrarily large sets A,BA,B with |A+B|≤K​|A||A+B|\leq K|A|.

Max–min distance ratio. The task places 1616 points in the plane to minimize the squared ratio between the maximum and the minimum pairwise distances. For example, the squared ratios 12.88912.889 and 13.013.0 in Table 1 correspond to the ratios 3.59023.5902 and 3.60563.6056.

Heilbronn problem for triangles. The task places 1111 points in the equilateral triangle with vertices (0,0)(0,0), (1,0)(1,0), and (1/2,3/2)(1/2,\sqrt{3}/2) to maximize the smallest area of the triangles formed by any three of the points, normalized by the area 3/4\sqrt{3}/4 of the equilateral triangle.

Kissing number in 1111 dimensions. A set of points C⊂ℝ11C\subset\mathbb{R}^{11} with 0∉C0\notin C and minx≠y⁡‖x−y‖≥maxx⁡‖x‖\min_{x\neq y}\|x-y\|\geq\max_{x}\|x\| over x,y∈Cx,y\in C yields a kissing configuration of |C||C| unit spheres. The task constructs such a set, and the score is the number of points |C||C|. The distances and norms are only used to check the validity of the configuration, and a configuration with more points than the known upper bound 868868 is rejected.

Circle packing. The task places 2626 non-overlapping circles in the unit square to maximize the sum of their radii. The evaluator checks the non-overlap and the containment of all circles, including that every radius is at most 0.50.5 and every center lies in the unit square, and checks that the sum of radii reported by the program agrees with the radii up to a relative and absolute tolerance of 10−310^{-3}.

Circle packing via linear programming. A variant of circle packing where the program proposes only the 2626 centers Ci∈[0,1]2C_{i}\in[0,1]^{2}, and the radii are recovered by a linear program that maximizes ∑iri\sum_{i}r_{i} subject to ri+rj≤‖Ci−Cj‖r_{i}+r_{j}\leq\|C_{i}-C_{j}\| and ri≤min⁡(Cix,Ciy,1−Cix,1−Ciy)r_{i}\leq\min(C_{i}^{x},C_{i}^{y},1-C_{i}^{x},1-C_{i}^{y}). The variant isolates the layout of the circles from the assignment of the radii. The starting code in the prompt solves the linear program with the HiGHS solver of SciPy.

Hadamard matrix. The task constructs a matrix H∈{±1}29×29H\in\{\pm 1\}^{29\times 29} that maximizes |det(H)|/(228⋅712⋅342)|\det(H)|/(2^{28}\cdot 7^{12}\cdot 342). Following the convention of Wang et al. (2026), the best-known construction with |det(H)|=228⋅712⋅320|\det(H)|=2^{28}\cdot 7^{12}\cdot 320 scores 320/342≈0.9357320/342\approx 0.9357.

I.2 Baselines

SCS. We use the implementation of SCS (Gideoni et al., 2026), which generates each program from a prompt containing the task instruction and 33 example programs sampled uniformly at random without replacement from the archive. SCS does not maintain an idea memory, and its prompt does not contain the summary of the idea memory used by ExpEvolve.

SCS+meta. SCS+meta adds the meta-summary of ShinkaEvolve to the prompt of SCS, i.e., a textual summary of the insights of recent programs with at most 55 recommendations, which is rewritten by DeepSeek-V4-Flash at temperature 00 after every generation, without the idea memory, the idea-guided actions, and the exploration at plateaus of ExpEvolve. It is run on First autocorrelation, Heilbronn, and Kissing with 1010 generations of 2020 programs, and on Uncertainty inequality with 2020 generations of 1010 programs.

ShinkaEvolve. We run ShinkaEvolve (Lange et al., 2026) with 55 islands and migration every 1010 generations, weighted parent sampling, an archive of 4040 programs, a meta-summary every 1010 generations with 55 recommendations, and both diff-based and full rewrites. ShinkaEvolve generates one program per generation, and does not distinguish the two configurations of ExpEvolve and SCS.

I.3 Budget and Resources

All methods evaluate each generated program once, and a failed program consumes the budget. The LLM calls of ExpEvolve for proposing, annotating, probing, and judging idea factors do not evaluate programs and do not consume the budget. Each run of ShinkaEvolve starts from 55 copies of the initial program, one for each island, and then generates 199199 programs, so its final performance is reported at 199199 generated programs. The evaluations of ExpEvolve and SCS are not limited in CPUs, while the runs of ShinkaEvolve on First autocorrelation, Second autocorrelation, Kissing, and Max–min distance ratio evaluate each program with at most 88 CPUs. The LLM is accessed either through the official API of DeepSeek or through OpenRouter, depending on the time of the run.

Per-seed results. Tables 5 and 6 report the final best score of each seed for the cells of Table 1, and Tables 7 and 8 report the best-so-far scores along the budget.

Prompt of a slot. The prompt of each slot is assembled as follows, where the strategy instruction is present only for idea-guided slots, and the summary of the idea memory is present for all slots.

At plateaus, the following note is prepended to the prompt of every slot, where {blur} lists the dependent idea factors as their names followed by the first 9090 characters of their descriptions, separated by semicolons, and {stall} is “best has stayed at {best} for {streak} generations”.

Annotator. The annotator LLM labels the idea factors of a program with the following prompt, where the descriptions are truncated to 200200 characters and the source code to 40004000 characters.

K.1 More Details of Experiments on Machine Learning Engineering

We further study whether the effectiveness of ExpEvolve transfers to machine learning engineering (MLE). We integrate its idea discovery and search control into OpenRSI (Yang et al., 2026b) and evaluate the resulting agent on MLS-Bench (Lyu et al., 2026a). This setting examines the use of idea factors within a harness that supports evolution on ML algorithms towards a specific task objective.

Tasks and data. MLS-Bench evaluates agents on improving components of ML algorithms under fixed task interfaces and evaluation protocols. Here we consider 6 tasks: Online bandit, Anomaly detection, Clustering, Multi-objective optimization, Subgroup calibration shift, and Evolution strategy. Search leverages the scores and execution feedback exposed by each task.

Backbone and budget. We use the evolutionary harness from OpenRSI, which organizes search through Draft, Improve, Debug, and Crossover operators. For each task, we retain a fixed history containing 20 completed search slots from an earlier OpenRSI run. The OpenRSI baseline and OpenRSI equipped with ExpEvolve continue from this same history for 50 additional evaluator calls, with 3 seeds. Both methods use 5 search slots per generation. All program generation uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. The same checkpoint performs factor discovery and annotation in ExpEvolve.

Integrating idea factors with OpenRSI. ExpEvolve initializes its idea memory from the shared history and updates it with newly evaluated programs. Consistent with Sec. 4, Discovery examines program pairs whose score differences are insufficiently explained by the current factors. The LLM reads their source and proposes reusable mechanisms. Factors zz enter the action catalog when both states have sufficient support and exhibit a score contrast in the archive. Each generation reserves two slots for Open exploration and schedules three for Guided search. Specifically, A guided slot first selects an action, such as 𝖠𝖣𝖣⁡(z)\mathsf{ADD}(z) or 𝖱𝖤𝖬𝖮𝖵𝖤⁡(z)\mathsf{REMOVE}(z), and then the harness selects a high-scoring parent compatible with that change. We use improvement over the best selected parent as action feedback, adapting the reward reference to OpenRSI’s parent–child structure. When the cumulative best score remains unchanged within relative tolerance 10−410^{-4} across three generation boundaries, ExpEvolve switches to idea-guided exploration at plateaus, aligning with Sec. 4.2.

Evaluation and results. We evaluate search performance using the best-so-far (BSF) score. For each task and method, we average the final BSF score over three seeds, starting from the same 20-slot history and continuing for 50 additional evaluations. Fig. 9(a) compares OpenRSI with OpenRSI+ExpEvolve across the six tasks. The reported configurations improve the mean final BSF score on all six tasks, with the largest gains on Online bandit and Anomaly detection.

Ethics Statement

This work studies evolutionary coding agents on open-ended mathematical discovery tasks and on machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. It does not involve human subjects or personally identifiable information, and all tasks come from public benchmarks or prior work.

Reproducibility Statement

The full procedure of ExpEvolve is given in Alg. 1 and Alg. 2, and its implementation details and hyperparameters are given in Appendix H and Table 3. The tasks, evaluators, and reference values are described in Appendix I.1, the configurations of the baselines in Appendix I.2, the budget and resources in Appendix I.3, the setting of MLS-Bench in Appendix K.1, and all prompts in Appendix K. The per-seed results are given in Appendix J. The formal statements and proofs of the theoretical results are given in Appendix E and Appendix F. All experiments on mathematical discovery use DeepSeek-V4-Flash unless stated otherwise, and each setting is run with 33 seeds.

AI Use Statement

We used LLM assistance to revise the manuscript’s organization and wording, identify and check related references, and examine the interpretation of reported experiments. The proposed framework itself uses LLMs to generate programs, propose idea factors, and assess program properties.
